first_delegated.default_label: range 40 to 500 as printed (40, 300, 400-500), scope per report

basis.text: Huey (6 Aug 1863) counts 150 wagons captured and Capehart (17 Aug 1863) 300 wagons and 15 ambulances taken, both present at the night attack; Lee, Stuart and Kilpatrick give 30 to 40 as the wagons carried off; 400 to 500 is a claim reported through a citizen.

default.label: 150 to 300 wagons captured or destroyed (Huey, Capehart); Lee's hearsay 40 and the 30 kept shown; range 40-500 listed

range.basis: the counts of wagons captured or taken by the two officers who wrote of it from the night attack (Huey 150; Capehart 300 wagons and 15 ambulances), possibly for different parts of one train; Lee's 40 is hearsay, the 40 and 30 of Stuart's citizen and Kilpatrick are wagons that stayed with the Union column, and 400 to 500 is a reported claim

default.basis_text: Lower end Huey (8th Pennsylvania Cavalry, report of 6 August 1863): 150 wagons captured at and near Monterey at 3 a.m.; upper end Capehart (1st West Virginia Cavalry, 17 August 1863): 300 wagons and 15 ambulances taken over about 8 miles. Neither says how he counted; they may be counting different parts of one train. Lee heard about 40 captured; Stuart's citizen and Kilpatrick give 40 and 30 that stayed with the Union column.

animation.note: Drawn at the low end of the sourced range, 150 (Huey). No source ranks Huey above Capehart; this is a drawing choice and is not a count. 300 and the ambulances stay selectable.

default.note: The figures of 40, 150, 300 and 400-500 count different things; the default keeps them apart and shows each with what it counts.

positions.label: About 40 wagons: Lee's hearsay figure of wagons captured; Stuart's citizen and Kilpatrick give 40 and 30 that stayed with the Union column

support.quote: a number of wagons, said to be about 40, were captured

witness.name: Robert E. Lee
witness.role: General commanding the Army of Northern Virginia (writing to President Davis near Hagerstown)

support.note: Lee to President Davis near Hagerstown, 4 days after (the text layer does not print this letter's dateline; the next letter, of July 8, begins 'My letter of yesterday'): 'In sending back our trains in advance, that of General Ewell was cut by the enemy's cavalry, and a number of wagons, said to be about 40, were captured.' A figure he had heard ('said to be') for wagons of Ewell's train captured; he was not at the pass. As a count of wagons captured it conflicts with 150 and 300.

support.quote: further informed [...] not more than 40 wagons

witness.name: J. E. B. Stuart
witness.role: Major General commanding the Cavalry Division; reached the pass the next day and heard a citizen's account

support.note: Stuart, after the campaign (the dateline of this part of his report is not printed in the text layer): a citizen told him Kilpatrick's cavalry had claimed several thousand prisoners and 400 or 500 wagons near Monterey, 'but I was further informed that not more than 40 wagons accompanied them', and other facts led him to think the success 'far overrated'. 40 is the number of wagons that went with the Union column, on a citizen's word, relayed.

support.quote: Ewell's large train was entirely destroyed, save eight forges, thirty wagons, and a few ambulances loaded with wounded rebel officers

witness.name: Judson Kilpatrick
witness.role: Brigadier General, commanding the Third Cavalry Division, leading the column through Monterey Pass

support.note: Kilpatrick, five weeks after: at daylight the train was entirely destroyed 'save eight forges, thirty wagons, and a few ambulances loaded with wounded rebel officers (sent with prisoners to Frederick City)'. Thirty is what was kept; he gives no count of the rest.

reason_not_chosen.text: Lee reports a hearsay figure of about 40 wagons captured; Stuart's citizen and Kilpatrick count 40 and 30 that stayed with the Union column. None was at the pass, or none counted the capture.

inference.step: Lee reports a figure he had heard ('said to be about 40') for wagons of Ewell's train captured; Stuart's citizen ('not more than 40 wagons accompanied them') and Kilpatrick ('thirty wagons' kept) count wagons that stayed with the Union column. The resolution reads the three as one small number; none of them says it was the whole capture.

support.quote: At 3 a. m. July 5, the wagon train was reached at and near Mon- terey, and 150 wagons captured

witness.name: Pennock Huey
witness.role: Colonel, 8th Pennsylvania Cavalry, commanding the Second Brigade, Second Division (Gregg's), sent to Kilpatrick on July 4; the rear of the column at Monterey Pass

support.note: Huey, a month after: at 3 a.m. on July 5 the wagon train was reached at and near Monterey and 150 wagons were captured (his report adds 1,600 prisoners; the text layer of one scan prints 1,500, so the prisoners are not used). He counts wagons captured, by his brigade or the column, not wagons destroyed; he does not say how the 150 were counted.

reason_not_chosen.text: 150 is Huey's count of wagons captured and is the lower end of the range of the two eyewitness counts that is the default.

support.quote: the whole train was taken — 300 wagons, 15 ambulances, together with all the horses and mules attached

witness.name: Charles E. Capehart
witness.role: Major, 1st West Virginia Cavalry, whose regiment led the charge on the train at Monterey Pass

support.note: Capehart, six weeks after: the road was interspersed with wagons and ambulances for 8 miles 'and the whole train was taken: 300 wagons, 15 ambulances, together with all the horses and mules attached'; prisoners 1,300. He counts wagons and ambulances taken, in the dark ('inky darkness' in the same report), and says 'the whole train'.

reason_not_chosen.text: 300 wagons and 15 ambulances is Capehart's count of the whole train taken and is the upper end of the range of the two eyewitness counts that is the default.

positions.label: 400 to 500 wagons: what Kilpatrick was said to have claimed (told to Stuart)

support.quote: Kilpatrick, who had claimed to have [...] several thousand prisoners and 400 or 500 wagons from our forces near Mon- terey

witness.name: J. E. B. Stuart
witness.role: Major General commanding the Cavalry Division; reached the pass the next day and heard a citizen's account

support.note: Stuart: what a citizen said Kilpatrick had claimed: 'several thousand prisoners and 400 or 500 wagons from our forces near Monterey', followed by Stuart's own doubt. No text of Kilpatrick's has this figure; his dispatch of July 5 says 'over 1,500 prisoners' and his report 1,360.

reason_not_chosen.text: Only a citizen's report of a claim, relayed by Stuart, who was not at the pass; Kilpatrick's own dispatch and report give no count of wagons captured or destroyed and say 1,500 and 1,360 prisoners, not several thousand.

inference.step: Stuart quotes a citizen who said Kilpatrick had claimed 400 or 500 wagons; the count is a claim as reported twice removed, not a count by anyone present.

positions.label: 37 wagons and 15 ambulances (a medical history says Kilpatrick reported it)

support.quote: Kilpatrick reported capturing 37 wagons and 15 ambulances

witness.name: Louis C. Duncan
witness.role: author of The Medical Department of the United States Army in the Civil War (1910s), a later history

support.note: A medical history of the 1910s, no page or source named in the text layer: 'Kilpatrick reported capturing 37 wagons and 15 ambulances loaded with wounded, and several hundred on foot.' Kilpatrick's report of 10 August 1863 and his dispatch of 5 July give no such figure; the 15 ambulances match Capehart's.
support.page_note: no printed page marks in the text layer; the passage is in the chapter on the retreat

reason_not_chosen.text: A history of the 1910s with no source named; neither Kilpatrick's dispatch of July 5 nor his report of August 10 has this figure.

inference.step: Duncan writes that Kilpatrick reported 37 wagons and 15 ambulances; this documents that Duncan wrote it; no report found carries the figure.

support.quote: a train consisting of more than one hundred wagons was over- taken at Monterey, on the road to Hagerstown, and captured, by Kilpatrick

witness.name: unnamed contributor, United States Service Magazine, January 1864
witness.role: a periodical of 1864, not a participant

support.note: A magazine of January 1864, no source named: 'a train consisting of more than one hundred wagons was overtaken at Monterey ... and captured, by Kilpatrick', part of it burnt to prevent recapture. A floor, not a count.
support.page_note: the text layer has no printed page marks; the passage is on page 76 of the volume (the running head UNITED STATES SERVICE MAGAZINE 76 stands in the text)

inference.step: The magazine says 'more than one hundred wagons'; read as a floor of 100, since it states no count.

reason_not_chosen.text: A floor ("more than", "over") given without a source; it is not a count, and it lies under the figures of the officers who were there.

weighing.summary: Huey (150 wagons captured) and Capehart (300 wagons and 15 ambulances taken) are officers of the best class of writing, present at the pass, writing within weeks; nothing separates them, so the count of wagons captured or destroyed is a range. Lee's 'about 40' is a figure he had heard, of wagons captured, and conflicts with both; the 40 of Stuart's citizen and the 30 of Kilpatrick count wagons that stayed with the Union column; the 400 to 500 is a claim reported by hearsay.
weighing.who: Huey and Capehart wrote as officers of Kilpatrick's column (a brigade at the rear; the regiment that led the charge). Kilpatrick commanded. Lee and Stuart were not at the pass: Lee writes what he heard from Ewell's side and Stuart what a citizen told him. The magazine, the guide and the medical history are not participants.
weighing.when: Huey 32 days, Capehart 43, Kilpatrick 36 days after; Lee 2 days, Stuart weeks after. The later figures are from 1864, 1892 and the 1910s, outweighed by reports of the time.
weighing.where: Capehart's regiment charged the train in the dark on the mountain road and says the train covered 8 miles; Huey's brigade came behind Custer and says the train 'was reached at and near Monterey' at 3 a.m. They may be counting different parts of one train, which is why the range stays; neither could count the whole, and neither says how he counted.
weighing.how_knew: Huey and Capehart give round numbers without a method; Kilpatrick counts the wagons he kept (thirty) because he took them away; Lee says "said to be"; Stuart repeats a citizen.
weighing.clock: Not applicable: a count has no clock; the reported difference of 20 minutes between the armies' clocks is not involved.
weighing.independence: Huey and Capehart are two separate groups (different brigades) and disagree; Huey's prisoners (1,500 or 1,600 by the scan) exceed the 1,360 Kilpatrick reports for the division, a doubt about Huey's counting, not a settlement. Lee's 40, Stuart's and Kilpatrick's figures are of the same small size but Lee's is a captured count heard second-hand and conflicts with 150 and 300; Lee and Stuart may relay each other. The magazine and the guide give floors with no source (positions P10, P11); the medical history is unsourced.

source_panel_text: Monterey Pass, night of Jul 4-5: two officers who were there count 150 wagons captured (Huey) and 300 wagons with 15 ambulances (Capehart), perhaps for different parts of the train. Lee heard about 40 captured; Stuart's citizen and Kilpatrick give 40 and 30 that stayed with the Union column. 400-500 is a claim told to Stuart. Range 150 to 300 shown.

pdf_default.note: 150 holds as the lower end of the range and as a sourced figure (Huey, p. 970; the first pass found no source for it). It does not hold as the one value: Capehart counts 300 and the plan's 40 and 400-500 count other things.

first_delegated.note: Range 40 to 500 joins wagons carried off (40), wagons captured or destroyed (150, 300) and a hearsay claim (400-500). The first pass also missed Huey's 150, so it called 150 unsourced.

what_would_change_it: A Confederate return of wagons lost by Ewell's or Rodes's train, a count by Kilpatrick, Custer, Richmond or Preston of the train taken, or a method for Huey's and Capehart's numbers would narrow or settle the range. A Confederate return of wagons lost would test Lee's hearsay 40.
